utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Wait for Mr...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is not -- Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow in a language that you can understand? This is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and good afternoon to you. Can you ask the technician because we don't have the LiveNote on the laptop, none of us. It's still on yesterday's. Perhaps if I connect -- no, it's still yesterday's. It's showing 6/11, which is yesterday. And the transcript is going on what is supposed to be yesterday. Sorry, Ms. Korner, appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought you were trying to economise on time. Mr. Ackerman, appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you want to adopt a new regimen, Your Honour, it is the same as it has been for days. John Ackerman, David Cunningham, and Mr. Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just one, Your Honour. And it's this: Your Honour, today we took a decision in respect of the disclosure to the Defence of the full transcripts of these summons interviews. Your Honour, having invited us to agree. In fact, we've taken on behalf of the Prosecution a unilateral decision that we will disclose the full transcript when we are notified by the Defence that the witness is actually intending to give evidence. Can I make it absolutely clear, this is not because we concede that the Defence has any right under the rules to full disclosure. But simply because the reality of the situation in this particular case is that where interviews were conducted with people as witnesses, they didn't get a copy of the interview. Where they were conducted as suspects, they did. And therefore, as a matter of practical reality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- It seems we should not withhold it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's a very practical approach, which I suppose Mr. Ackerman will accept without -- it being submitted, offered, and accepted on without prejudice on both sides. Okay? Mine, I think, yes, now it's okay. Madam Chuqing has got expert hands. Yes, Ms. Korner, let's bring the witness in and you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, to you, Mr. Radic. We are going to proceed with the cross-examination, and then re-examination, and hopefully finish. Much depends on you. When I see that you are beating around the bush, I am going to call your attention. If you don't heed my word, I will let you continue, but the price you will pay for that is that you won't be out of here before Monday or Tuesday or Wednesday of next week. So it's up to you. Answer the questions as yes, no, or as required, without going around the bush, and without requiring for this and for that if you know that you are in a position to give the answer. Ms. Korner, please. We will try to finish with the witness today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Ms. Korner: [Continued].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I want to move to the regional crisis staff which was established formally on the 5th of May 1992. You accept you were a member of that crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The number of meetings you attended, you think, was not high. But without seeing the minutes, you are unable to say exactly how many.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did, however, attend the first meeting?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you told us that if you couldn't attend, you would send your secretary?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you to please just confirm what you told us about the crisis staff -- the regional crisis staff in interview. It's page 8 of the first interview which is up on the screen. In the B/C/S version, it's page 9. And it will be handed to you. It has been highlighted. You were shown the document that established the crisis staff, and you said: "It was confirmed at the assembly" - this is line 22 of the English - "actually, he was the president. It was confirmed at the assembly, and the executive committee of the ARK. It was signed by Mr. Erceg." It was put to you: "Once the crisis staff came into existence on the 5th of May 1992, it was the highest authority as far as a governing body in the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Correct?" You said: "Yes, because the assembly of the autonomous region was then disbanded so that the only thing that remained were the assemblies of towns." Then you were asked how the crisis staff functioned in relation to these assemblies. If we go to page 9, it was put to you by the questioner: "I want to stay focussed in the crisis staff of the autonomous region, was the highest body of government authority at the time once the assembly was disbanded. Is that correct?" Answer: "Yes." Question: "And the ARK crisis staff had direct control over the municipalities within the ARK. Is that correct?" And you said: "Depending. It depended on the individual. It depended on the people in the municipalities. It varied because there are documents from which you can tell when exactly we -- because the municipal assembly still existed when Banja Luka resisted certain questions." I'm sorry, "decisions." I can't read my own... And then there were some further questions, and you were asked about the decisions. It was put to you: "The regional crisis staff issued decisions which were then transmitted to the municipal crisis staffs." You disagreed. You were asked: "In that case, what was the purpose of the issuing of decisions if they weren't going to the municipal?" And you then explained, and I'm summarising your answer, that they only existed, you thought, then between the beginning of April until the corridor was opened, and then they were disbanded. And you were asked again to see the crisis staffs. Do you accept that those are the answers that you gave?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is exactly what I said at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to put it to you that one day on which you definitely attended was the 18th of May 1992. And I'll show you the -- I'd like you to have now P227. And I'll give you the B/C/S copy that has actually been marked for the meeting of the 18th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry, Madam Registrar. I'll hand over my copy. There it is. I've marked it with a... It's number 12 at the bottom of the page that you are now going to get. Your Honour, I make it clear the suggestion I'm putting is based on part of Exhibit 759.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 18th of May, a number of matters were discussed including an assertion, if you like, in number 2 of the conclusions: "The crisis staffs are now the highest organs of the authority -- of authority in the municipalities." Presumably, Mr. Radic, you agreed with that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I know that's what it says. But as far as you were concerned, the crisis staff in Banja Luka was at this stage at the highest level of authority until such time as the assembly verified the decisions?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The assembly stopped functioning, and the crisis staff was supposed to make decisions which fall within the purview of the municipal assembly's duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look, please, at item number 15, this is over the page, or conclusion number 15, where a meeting is to be held in Mrkonjic Grad with a delegation from Jajce and the delegation of the autonomous region consisting of Mr. Kupresanin, Mr. Erceg, yourself, Mr. Brdjanin, Mr. Sajic, and Mr. Zupljanin. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having attended this meeting, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'm suggesting to you that you were. But I'm now asking you whether or not you recall holding a meeting in Mrkonjic Grad with people from Jajce?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at a meeting with people from Jajce, but this was not in Mrkonjic Grad, but in Banja Luka. And it was at their request. As for my meeting them in Mrkonjic Grad, I can't remember that I met them there. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And the final one on this -- the final one on this particular meeting, number 18, Karadzic, Koljevic, Krajisnik, Subotic, and Mladic to have talks with representatives of the Autonomous Region of Krajina on Monday, the 25th of May. Do you remember these people coming down at around that period?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam Prosecutor, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You can give that back because that's all I want to ask you about the decisions. I just want to deal with a few more things that you said during the course of the interview about the regional crisis staff. Page 35 in English of the first interview. In the B/C/S version, page 36. And it should be highlighted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm wondering if I might be excused for five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Do you require the sitting to stop?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not just feeling real well, and I think I can be excused for five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, what I meant was whether you want us to stop for these five, ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think not. I think you might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, yes. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will see, I think it's highlighted for you, it's line 22 in the English of page 35, you mentioned that the ARK president had visited many of the municipalities in the region. It's also true that the local municipality presidents were also summoned to Banja Luka. Is that correct? And I think you just made a noise. And it was put to you: "And in fact, met with the ARK Crisis Staff on a regular basis. And you replied, they were also members of the crisis staff. Question: "I'm talking about the local municipality crisis staff presidents. They regularly reported to Banja Luka and gave situation reports on events occurring in their area of responsibility. Is that correct?" And you said: "Yes." Do you agree that you said that in interview?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were meetings at which presidents of municipalities submitted briefings on what was going on in various areas. That is a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can I just ask you this: Were there, in fact, two sets of meetings held by the regional crisis staff; the first where the actual core members met, and the second where the presidents of the municipalities came, much bigger meetings?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only remember a few meetings with the presidents of the municipalities. Now, whether those were joint meetings or separate meetings, I can't tell you. There were meetings together with representatives of the municipalities who were talking about what was going on on the edges of the territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And finally, then, at page 53, on the same topic effectively, and in the B/C/S, it's page 54, only seems to be one page ahead. Question: You were being asked about -- the same topic, the meetings attended by presidents of the municipality. It was put to you: "You've told us that when there were problems in municipalities, the leaders of the municipality would attend a meeting of the regional crisis staff." And you replied: "Sometimes." Then there was a break and the tape was changed. You were asked: "Was there a discussion of the problem?"? "On the problem of the municipality, yes." "When a decision was made, that decision was then made, was it not, by Mr. Brdjanin?" And you said: "Most often, yes." Again, did you say that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not reading this. What I have in front of me it something completely different. It is page 53 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 54.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you saying --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 54. I'm sorry. I thought I said it. Page 54 and 55. It's the bottom of 54, I think, and into page 55.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the question was whether they came when they had problems. Yes, they did. They discussed their problems. They sought decisions. And decisions were taken at such meetings. And when the decisions were made, they were made by Mr. Brdjanin. It was not Mr. Brdjanin alone who could make a decision of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but try to answer the question. Don't go beyond the question. The question was whether you stated this. And your answer should have been yes or no. And then if you wanted to explain your something, you put your hand and ask for my permission.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next question I was going to ask you "is that correct?" And you say now it couldn't be made by Mr. Brdjanin alone. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said most often, the rest of it was -- I didn't understand. But what I'm saying is I think that it was not up to him to make these decisions on helping them on his own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that's what I'm asking you. What do you mean by that? You added that now, so I'm asking you what you mean.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He couldn't make those decisions on his own. If there is a meeting, then a number of people participate in making such decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Radic, I'm sure you're absolutely right. There was discussion in these meetings involving a number of people. But when a decision had to be made, whether supplies should be given to a particular municipality or some kind of aid, was that made by Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Together with others, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had the last say, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. That's all I want to ask you about that. Now, I want to move to this question of the police. And as you told this Court and as you said in interview, you firmly assert that no one in civilian authorities could give orders to the police. That's what you say, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, as the president, no, but there was a ministry within the civilian bodies. If you don't consider the ministry to be a civilian body, then no. But the ministry could issue such instructions. But not municipal representatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, would you accept that whether it was direct orders or by way of influence, the views and wishes of the, first of all, regional crisis staff were respected by the police?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, I'm going to object to the form of that question because it calls for orders or by way of influence. There's a difference between the two, and I would object in Mr. Ackerman's absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But she -- Ms. Korner did not say "and." She said "or." So the witness is in a position or free to address himself to either of those two and give an answer. It wasn't put to him in a combined manner. It's in the alternative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Radic, what's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the president of the crisis staff could attempt to exert an influence. But the Ministry of the Interior in Pale had the final decision. But an attempt could be made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: More than an attempt, couldn't it? Successful, and I'll use the word orders, which were carried out by the police were given, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could receive a decision from the crisis staff. But then it was up to them to decide how to operate with the agreement of the Ministry of the Interior. But they could receive a decision from the crisis staff. In any case, this happened on one occasion, and it is recorded in a document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll come on to some documents in a moment. But wasn't it actually the case, whether because the Ministry of the Interior told the police to do this, that the police did carry out instructions given to them by -- and now let me deal -- by the municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the municipal authorities, no. They weren't implemented. They weren't duty-bound to implement them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the regional? Would the police carry out, as far as you were concerned, instructions given to them by the regional authorities? That is, either the assembly or the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But in a modified form, and this is recorded in a document when Mr. Zupljanin said "not without my knowledge." You're not going to modify without me being aware of it. I have to be aware of who is going to be replaced. And it is for me to say who is going to be replaced, if you can remember that. So they modified the order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us to what document you're referring?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You showed it to me yesterday or the day before yesterday. I can't remember any more. But first of all, it said what the crisis staff had decided, and then it said what Zupljanin told the police to do. There must have been consultations with the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to show you then -- in fact, I'm going to go back to that document. Can you look, however, first at P202, and to save any wasting time here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Usher, needn't bother. The B/C/S, I've highlighted the B/C/S. Do Your Honours have it, or do you want it up on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we better have it on the ELMO. It will save time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Usher, you'll need to put the English on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're full of exhibits here, have them at the right, the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you could put the first page on the ELMO, first. In fact, I forgot to give that to Mr.... It's the right one. Could you give that to Mr. Radic, please, usher. Usher. Sorry. I only gave the back part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, that's the front of this document dated the 20th of May 1992. It's the conclusions of a meeting held on the 6th of May 1992. Attending that meeting apart from Mr. Zupljanin were the chiefs, as you can see in the first paragraph, of Banja Luka, Gradiska, Dubica, so on and so forth. And then if we go to the page that I highlighted for you - usher, that's page 4 in the English version - this is Mr. Zupljanin issuing instructions. Paragraph 23: "In all our activities, we are obliged to observe all measures and apply all procedures ordered by the crisis staff of the autonomous region. With regard to disarmament, when the deadline of weapons surrender expires on 11th May 1992, we should take no action until the crisis staff makes the relevant decisions." Were you aware that those instructions had been given by Mr. Zupljanin to the chiefs of all, as far as we can tell, all the SJBs within his area of influence?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam, because he didn't forward such things to the presidents of municipalities, but the representatives of municipalities, but only to SJBs that were under his jurisdiction. But there is still a question as to when he received the order from the crisis staff and whether he consulted the Ministry of the Interior. I can't see that this text mentioned it. It should be analysed, examined to see whether he asked for the agreement of the Ministry of the Interior. I don't think that he was able to do so on an independent basis without the Ministry of the Interior being aware of this. This is my opinion. I can't claim this for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may well be right, Mr. Radic. All that I am putting to you is that your assertion and that of many other witnesses, I have to tell you, that the civilian authorities had no ability to order or instruct the police is simply not right.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to make a distinction between civilian authorities. You're referring to municipal authorities, and in that case I'm claiming they weren't in a position to do this. But If you're referring to the Ministry of the Interior, if that's what you mean by civilian authorities, then absolutely, they were in a position to act in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I don't mean the Ministry of the Interior. I'm showing you a document where Mr. Zupljanin says that they are obliged to observe all measures and apply all procedures ordered by the crisis staff of the region. And I'm putting it to you, Mr. Radic, that you knew full well that that is -- even if you didn't see this document, that the police were applying the instructions of the regional crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have a document which demonstrates that I really knew about this, that they could have implemented these decisions and that they did implement them, I'd like you to show it to me. But I'm telling you that I wasn't aware of them being obliged to carry out decisions of the crisis staff without having consulted the Ministry of the Interior. This is my experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is that what you see over there proves you wrong, that you had the wrong idea, or wrong opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm suggesting, Your Honour -- I want to be absolutely clear. I'm suggesting that the opinion expressed by Mr. Radic is not at all a true opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what you are suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm suggesting that he knew full well, but doesn't want to say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's move ahead, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will show you another document, not all of the ones we have, Mr. Radic, to show you exactly what we mean. P271, and together with P272. 271 first. This is a dispatch from the CSB, Mr. Zupljanin, sent to, again, all SJBs dealing with the order by the regional crisis staff to disarm paramilitaries. Paragraph number 1: "Weapons and ammunition returned voluntarily in response to the order issued by the crisis staff of the autonomous region should be classified according to type." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the text in front of me, yes. I understand it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you look now, please, at P272, this is another order being sent to the SJBs dated the 6th of July 1992. And there, you will see that the crisis staff -- the SJBs are being sent the decision about dismissals of the 22nd of June. Now, Mr. Radic, one more time, after seeing these documents which I assure you are a sample, it is the case, isn't it, that the police followed the instructions issued by the regional crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusion from this can be drawn that Radoslav Brdjanin forwarded such an order to the chief of the CSB, the Security Services Centre, for it to be implemented. I don't know what else I should say. This is clearly demonstrated by the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And he forwarded it to the SJBs for implementation. That's what this document shows, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can we deal now with Prijedor. If you have back the exhibit you were shown. Actually I think it was 1195, although Mr. Ackerman gave it a Defence number, but it doesn't matter. It's the same exhibit. This is a meeting in fact of the SDS municipal board, not particularly the police, but we're going to deal with the document on the police in a moment. Do you see Mr. Kovacevic, what he had to say? Sorry, I didn't mark this, but it should be -- Mr. Kuruzovic spoke first, and then Mr. Kovacevic explaining: "The cabinet meets daily and has adopted at least 50 decisions. And then replacement of staff had been carried out." And you were asked about that because it's before the June instruction. "The functioning of government at the level of Krajina can now be felt. Instructions and decisions are being forwarded from the top." Now, you assert that nobody had any control over Prijedor. Is that what you're asserting?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police and the CSB could have had partial control up until a certain period of time. The CSB, the Security Services Centre to which Prijedor belonged could have had control over the police part. But this is the municipal board of the SDS. They would hold sessions, and they would adopt decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, the truth is although - and I accept entirely - Prijedor didn't like the authority of the regional crisis staff, they did carry out their instructions, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which instructions you are referring to. But what they did was not in accordance with any of the instructions that were being adopted and of which I was aware. But in Prijedor, I'd say that they would take autonomous decisions of the SDS and of the police, and the regional staff had very little influence over them. Almost none at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. One final document on this topic: P1294, please. This is a document of the 13th of July addressed to the Autonomous Region of Krajina, I think. And it's a report on the implementations of the conclusions of the Prijedor municipal crisis staff. There are a number of conclusions. Can you turn to the very end of paragraph 1, which is on the second page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know where it comes from but it's addressed to the Autonomous Region of Krajina. I can't find that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we see the first page again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't believe it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm also claiming that that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What a surprise. I don't really mind, Your Honour, whether it's addressed to them or not because the report in itself will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Korner ought not to make representations in the record as to what a document stands for when it doesn't. She says it was addressed to the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and I don't think it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, yes, yes. But we have two conflicting statements, or not exactly conflicting. Go ahead, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree. I don't think it matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not proposing to argue on this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The end of paragraph 1: "The decision of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Banja Luka - and it gives the number, dated the 22nd of June, that's the infamous decision on dismissing people - on filling vacant management and other posts valid for the running of the economy was implemented in the public security stations." Can you go to the end of paragraph 2, which is on our page 3 in the English: "The calculation and payment of salaries for the month of May" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I think there seems to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll give you the full decision. I don't know why you haven't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you mean the exhibit is missing? That's good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we have it or don't we have it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's not this here, can I read it out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Conclusions and the public community is responsible for implementing it. It gives a number. They're requesting from the public utilities institute to provide the rules on systematisation and information for paying salaries, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were unaware that the Court doesn't appear to have the full exhibit. If you go to the end, go to the second, I imagine it's the second or third page, of paragraph 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's at the bottom of page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The page with 7106 at the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will see: "The calculation and payment of salaries for the month of May done in consultation with the director of the Prijedor SDK and on the basis of the decision of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." Right, can we go, please, to number 7. Paragraph 7, please. "On the basis of the conclusion" - number given - "dated 10th of June 1992 and with regard to the conclusion of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Banja Luka, all socially owned enterprises must start working in accordance with wartime plans." Mr. Radic, you were shown in interview -- you can give that document back now to the usher -- and can we go to the second interview, please, page 16. That same exhibit. And in the B/C/S of the second interview, it's page 15. You were shown that document during that interview. It was read out to you, and the questioner said to you: "Now, Mr. Radic, that, in respect of the municipality of Prijedor" - this was on the 22nd of June decision - "again is a euphemism for dismissing non-Serbs in this case from positions in the public security station, isn't it?" You said: "This is a systemisation of positions in the public security service in the police." And then you said: "I don't remember because I neither sent nor implemented it." And it was put to you: "No, I realise you had nothing to do with it. But again, from your knowledge of events, this was essentially Prijedor getting rid of or confirming that non-Serbs had been removed from the police force. Correct?" And you said: "If this is what Mr. Cayley is talking about, and from this it will be very difficult for the Prosecutor to prove that this is about non-Serbs. And that's why I'm calling it a euphemism. And the balancing of staff, it says systemisation here, but it never says who is in question. And even the person who replied to it never said it was non-Serb population that was dismissed." "It was," and whatever you said then was unintelligible, "but let me tell you, the fact is it was them who were dismissed." Now, can you go to page 19 -- or can we go to page 19, and for you in the B/C/S page 18 -- page 17, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I say something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you have read out, I didn't have that in front of me. I had page 15 in front of me, and it contains something quite different. Everything you just read out is not something I had before me. So could that please be placed in front of me. Could I please be provided with the document. I was looking at page 15, and that's not what it says there, what you just read out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He got the -- I said the second interview, and he was given the first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The first, right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to read it out again. You can read it yourself, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's page 15, and it should be highlighted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go to page 15, Mr. Radic. And read it for yourself. Don't read aloud because you will confuse the interpreters. Confuse, not in a derogatory meaning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Prosecutor, I stand by what I said when I said there is no list and that I can't see who was dismissed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you now to look, please, at page 19 of that interview, which should be -- I'm sorry, for you page 17, and our page 19, second interview. It's on the screen as well. Question: "When the Prijedor Crisis Staff is saying that individuals had been removed from the police force pursuant to this decision, they were implementing a decision of the ARK Crisis Staff, weren't they?" Your answer: "Implicitly, yes. It comes from this document there. Yeah, implicitly, yes, because this document says this was done on the other document pursuant to this decision." Then you were asked about the signature block of Mr. Brdjanin, you had already said in your view, and you've told us it's not signed by him, the decision of the 22nd of June, and you suggest that a graphologist compares the signatures. And then further on, the top of page 18 for you, and the bottom of page 19 for us: "The orders that were coming to the Prijedor Crisis Staff were implemented" -- I'm sorry. The question was before that. "Just pure logic, looking at this purely logically, these two documents taken together demonstrate that the Prijedor Crisis Staff recognised the authority of the ARK Crisis Staff." Your reply: "The orders that were coming to Prijedor Crisis Staff were implemented." Then the question: "And that is orders that were coming from the ARK crisis staff. Correct?" And you said: "It's visible from that previous document." And then it was put to you that there were other documents that show the same thing, but I don't think we need to tuggle with that. Now, it's right, isn't it, Mr. Radic, and I'm asking you this as somebody who was there and attended at least some of the meetings of the regional crisis staff, that the major decisions made by the regional crisis staff, dismissals and disarmament and the like, were implemented by the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends. In certain cases, in some places, they were fully implemented, and some places they weren't. As far as Prijedor was concerned, I think that they introduced many of their own decisions and implemented things in their own manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're saying, as I understand it, Mr. Radic, Prijedor went even further than most municipalities?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is -- I'm sorry. Go on.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Though I can only draw this conclusion on the basis of what happened, but not on the basis of their decisions because I do not have their decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's to your knowledge, isn't it, that the worst crimes that were committed virtually within the Krajina were committed in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to look at two other aspects of this passing on of orders. Could you now in that very same interview go to page 47, please. I'm sorry, for you, page 43, I think. For us, page 47. At the bottom of our page 47, and the conversation before that had been about the disarmament operation, went as follows: "So it was the ARK Crisis Staff essentially passing on orders from above to the municipalities?"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I should add here that that was not actually apparently translated, the next line, "within the Krajina that led to this disarmament operation." So the only thing that was said in B/C/S are the first words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you just confirm, Mr. Radic, what is actually said to you there is: "So it was the ARK Crisis Staff essentially passing on orders from above to the municipalities?" Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we can say that the crisis staff issued those orders to other crisis staffs. There is nothing about municipalities here. There are just three dots and a question mark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give me back -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I see what he's looking at. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read out line 24, the first part in green, without adding anything. Just read that the sentence as written there, please, read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "That means we may say that the crisis staff issued those orders from below to other crisis staffs." A few dots, question mark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From below, right. Well, that's... All right. I think we'll have to have another look at that. But anyhow, could you read out, please, the answer you gave, Mr. Radic, as it is written there.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Not issued orders, just forwarded what they themselves got. I don't want you to think that the decisions were drafted in the crisis staff. What we received we forwarded, and that was that." And what is this so much about that, after that a dash, a question mark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's handle it in a different manner. Can I ask the interpreters to look at lines 26 to 28 on page 43, what you have on -- yes, exactly, what's going to be highlighted. And translate those words into English without referring to the corresponding English text that you have on the screen. I just would like to have a free translation of that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "It didn't send. It forwarded what they had received. I don't want you to think that this decision was drafted in the crisis staff. What we received, we forwarded. That was that. And what is this? So much --?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I've raised this because in the English version, Ms. Korner, there is clearly "from above," two words which the witness omitted when he was reading himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I have now a confirmation from the interpreters that those words --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, what's been translated was the answer the witness gave, and it's the question that has the words "from above."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. That's the answer. The answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's comment, the word "from above" is actually in line 24, but it is not "from above", but "from below".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. But if you read, Ms. Korner, Mr. Radic's answer in the English version, lines 25 onwards, it says: "No, not that they gave, but that they forwarded what they were given from above." The words "from above" do not show up in the Bosnian or Serbian text. This is what I wanted to make clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They do show up, but he didn't read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no they don't show up in the original -- in the Serbian text which is lines 26 to 28 of page 43 or whatever, what should be the corresponding words to "from above" do not exist. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. I follow that. All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the only thing we can do, Mr. Radic, is clear up now what you were saying. Were you saying there to the interviewers that you forwarded the instruction -- as a member of the regional crisis staff instructions that were received from above, and by above, I mean from the republic level, were being forwarded to the municipal level?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was saying is that decisions were not drafted in the crisis staff. They were received, and then they were forwarded. But not to the municipalities, but to the municipal secretariats for National Defence or for the Territorial Defence. They were the ones who were in charge of implementing those decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the case of the Defence, which is what you were being asked about there. That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in line 30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, in respect of the decisions that were -- we've seen from the regional crisis staff forwarded from -- to municipal -- either SJBs or the municipal crisis staffs, were those instructions dreamed up by the region on its own or were they as a result of instructions coming from Pale?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, the crisis staffs did not create anything. They just forwarded what they received from a higher level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I'm talking -- forget about the municipal crisis staff. I'm talking specifically now about the regional crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The regional crisis staff also had to receive an order from somebody to the effect of carry out disarmament. It was not within its purview to do that. So I suppose they must have received that order from somebody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the dismissals instruction? Was that something that originated entirely from the region, from, I suggest, Mr. Brdjanin, or was it something that came from Pale?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a matter of general policy, and the response to what had happened on other sides, on the opposition sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to just deal very briefly, please, then with the army and what you said about that in interview. You personally were very concerned, weren't you, with the supplying of the light brigades in the Banja Luka area, within the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Supplying clothing, food, accommodation, all of that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as I think you've already told us, and we may not need to look at the interview for this, General Talic certainly attended the first meeting of the regional crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he attended one meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And thereafter, he sent a representative, normally Colonel Vojinovic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojinovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So sorry. I keep mispronouncing his name. And just one moment. I'll just see if I need to put this. I don't want to waste time if I don't have to. Here, can I put to you, and you can look at it if you like, Mr. Radic, but it's page 47 of the first interview. And page 48, I'm sorry, in the B/C/S. And it should be highlighted. The first -- you were asked: "Did you attend meetings in the conference room behind your own office?" There had been discussion where the meetings were being held. And you said: "I think I was at one. I think that was the first one where Mr. Talic was also present. That was the only time he attended. When that meeting was held and General Talic attended, was there discussion about looting that was taking place and the disappearance of people?" Your answer: "For the most part, from what I remember of the time that Talic was present, we talked about supplying the military with food and also preventing crime and things like that." Do you agree that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to deal briefly then, please, with the subject of the camps, particularly those in Prijedor. You knew, didn't you, Mr. Radic, you'd heard about and that's why you went there, the camps in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about the camp, and that's when we went there to see what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was common knowledge, wasn't it, in Banja Luka through refugees who were coming there that there were three major camps in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was common knowledge that there were camps, but we did not know the nature -- what the nature of those camps was. And they asked us in Banja Luka to provide accommodation for these people whom they had detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, isn't it true that, first of all, the camp at -- established in this china factory -- ceramics factory, Keraterm, just on the outskirts of Prijedor, that was known about in Banja Luka, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know you didn't go there, but you'd heard about it, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd heard of Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you told us when you were asked about this by Mr. Ackerman on the first day that - and this is at page 49 of the LiveNote - that there had been an invitation from the Prijedor people to visit the camps. You said that you believed the invitation was sent to Mr. Brdjanin who then invited all of us to go there together.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your way to Prijedor, did you pass through the areas that had been destroyed around Kozarac and the like?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we went by Kozarac. You had to go by Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was clear, wasn't it, that there had been wholesale destruction of the housing owned by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kozara was within the area of war operations, and it was not just Muslims there. There were also Serbs. Yes, and it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This wasn't war operations, wasn't it? This was houses that had been torched, set on fire deliberately?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, there was fighting that was conducted from these houses. But you would have to ask those who were involved in those war operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was noticeable, wasn't it, that the Serb houses, those owned by Serbs, were still standing untouched?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I didn't know which houses were Serbian houses, which ones are Muslim houses. But there are also Croat houses there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Destroyed?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, torched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to summarise what you told us. You told us that what you saw in Omarska appalled you. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So much so that you kicked a stone to express your rage as you came out of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not the only expression of my feelings. But this is something that I recall and that others who were with me on that day recall as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And though you didn't see inside any of the buildings, you said you believed, and this is at page 54, that there were more of them indoors. Why did you believe there were more of them indoors?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because according to the information that I had, there should have been more people than those that were standing in front of the building, in the area between the hangar and the admin building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the conditions in there, and this was the end of your sentence. You said: "I believe there are more of them indoors, and the conditions in there were not very good." How did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was very hot, and the building was -- it was made of metal. It was very hot outside, and I could only imagine how it must have been inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Weren't you surprised that the Prijedor authorities were asking you and Mr. Brdjanin and other people to come and look at such an appalling camp?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a very precise goal in mind when they invited us. They didn't know what to do with these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they had to talk to the International Committee of the Red Cross, and up to then, they had refused to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told them they had to talk to the International Committee of the Red Cross, they having refused to do that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you pointed out, did you, to them that these conditions were unfit for human beings to live in?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the Red Cross was much better equipped to deal with the situation than they themselves. At least they could do much better than they did in that particular place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Did you point out to Dr. Stakic and Mr. Drljaca and Mr. Kovacevic that human beings should not be held in these kind of conditions?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Drljaca and Mr. Kovacevic were not there on that occasion. It was only Stakic, the president of the municipal assembly, who was there. And some of his associates who were also there on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you told us that Mr. Brdjanin noticed that you were very angry about this. And he didn't say very much and just mentioned the fact that you kicked the stone. But you said at page 56: "The mere fact that he, that is Mr. Brdjanin, mentioned it, that he told me, that means that he agreed with me and that he also agreed that the way these people were treated was not right. That is my assumption." Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my assumption. When we returned, he told some people how angry I was about what I'd seen. That means that he had noticed what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he himself expressed no anger at all. Is that the situation?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't claim that for a fact. I don't know whether he did or whether he didn't. But I'm sure that he must have had some opinion about what he had seen. I can't say that for a fact because I was not in the position to observe very clearly what was going on around me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. But you were with Mr. Brdjanin at the camp, and you were with Mr. Brdjanin at the municipal building. At any time in your hearing did he express any horror or disgust at what he had seen?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether he expressed horror, anything like that. All I know is that he did not oppose me when I said that I would warn Mr. Beat Schweitzer, the representative of the Red Cross, about what was going on and that I would tell him this had to be dealt with as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told him it was your intention to get in touch with the Red Cross as soon as possible to notify them that they should go into that camp?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look again, please, at the newspaper report that you were shown by Mr. Ackerman, which is -- it's Exhibit 284. You've got the marked copy? And we've marked the part that we want you to look at. And now I've lost my own English copy. This is the report in Kozarski Vjesnik of the 17th of July. I would like you to go to the marked part.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And usher, could we have, please, on the ELMO page 2 of the English. If you haven't got it there, you can use this copy and I can read from the ELMO. Could you just put it down slightly for a moment. The other way. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After they had made a tour of the combat area and collection centres, the visitors from Krajina thanked their hosts for their hospitality and efforts in creating a new Serbian state in that area, especially at these fateful times when Alija Izetbegovic was confident he has established a new Alcatraz in Prijedor. "Radoslav Brdjanin: What we have seen in Prijedor is an example of a job well done. And it is a pity that many in Banja Luka are not aware of it yet, just as they are not aware of what might happen in Banja Luka in the very near future." Mr. Radic, did you think that what had happened in Prijedor, the camps and the like was a job well done?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a job well done. I must say that nobody prepared any accommodation for the refugees, and I don't think that this was a job well done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, if we go on we see that there was a briefing from Colonel Arsic, Dr. Stakic, Kovacevic, Drljaca. So you saw him back at the municipal building. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then apparently you spoke about the significance of the events in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Usher, could you pull that up slightly so I can see the next paragraph. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "At present, we need Banja Luka as a logistics centre. We are doing everything and will continue to do everything to preserve peace in Banja Luka despite threats, various threats, and attempts to disrupt it. In the Croatian, Austrian, and German media, Banja Luka has been accused as -- has been accused of persecuting the Muslims and the Croats. Our adversaries resort to every possible kind of lie. But in spite of that, we are not giving in. Unfortunately, we do not have solutions for many problems. Among those are refugees and collection centres. The International Red Cross has been trying for days to reach Prijedor, but we said that we shall provide them access only after they personally have examined the situation of the Serbian refugees and prisoners in Odzak, Rascani, Travnik, Zenica, Sarajevo, Konjic, and many other places." Is that what you said, Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I inquire if the Prosecution is putting to Mr. Radic that it is not the case that he reported what he saw there to the ICRC? Is that the effort that's being made?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Answer the question first, and then we come to your point, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Answer the question that Ms. Korner put. I'm sorry, I apologise. Answer the question that Ms. Korner put to you. I'll read the question myself. Or rather, you put it again, Ms. Korner, it's easier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what you said to the newspapers, Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already said that. The International Red Cross had indeed tried to reach Prijedor for days. But they were prevented from doing that, but not by us, but by those who were in charge of those camps at the time. But I also said that they should go and look at the people in Rascani and Odzak and so on and so forth and liberate them. Eventually this was done. Prijedor was the first. What I was saying was that there shouldn't be a difference made between the camps holding Serbs and between the camps holding Bosniaks in Prijedor. That was what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you only have one or more questions on this particular topic which you would like to put now, you may proceed. Otherwise, we stop here and have the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I've just got one further question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, you'd come back to me with my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe we better have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think it is obvious because he answered in a way which also confirms that he did speak to the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, you're not feeling well, and you have been abandoned by everyone?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. One of those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, there, everyone is coming back. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You still got the article there, have you, Mr. Radic? What I simply want to know is whether you said that you would provide access to Prijedor for the Red Cross only after they had looked into the situation of camps which held Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. We had informed them of what was happening in Rascani, Odzak, and Samac a lot earlier. So I told them to go to Prijedor, but that they should also deal with Rascani, which they subsequently did. You have a document on the release of Serbs from Rascani. So we noticed that treatment wasn't the same for those who were detained in Rascani, Odzak, and in Prijedor. So there weren't any conditions, but they did release the people, the detainees from Prijedor first after all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To cut short this topic, Mr. Radic, isn't the reality that the Red Cross only got into these camps, that is, Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje, after their conditions had been revealed to the world by the ITN News journalists?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when the world found out about it. But I do know that I spoke to members of the International Red Cross and that they said that they had serious problems with regard to registering people who were in Omarska because they weren't allowed to do this. They subsequently went there and registered them. But whether this was after this was made public, I don't know. But you can be sure that they had precise information about what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm suggesting to you in the clearest possible terms, Mr. Radic, that only after the 5th of August when the ITN News crew went there were any of the International Red Cross able to get into the camps as a result of negotiations with Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Only he could have given an order and allowed any crew of journalists to enter. I could only ask them and say that they should be allowed to enter as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you say that sometime between the 17th of July and the 5th or 6th of August, you spoke to Mr. Schweitzer from the International Red Cross in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you indicated that he should go into Omarska?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he explain to you that they had been trying to get into Omarska and Keraterm and Trnopolje without any success?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions he told me that he couldn't get in to those camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you think of raising the matter with Mr. Brdjanin to see whether or not he could have some influence on the authorities in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You can take the article away, and could I have my copy back, please. Now, the crisis staff decisions, the regional crisis staff decisions, were verified on the 17th of July. Did you hear Mr. Brdjanin on Radio Banja Luka on the 18th of July of 1992, the day after the verification of the decisions?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember listening to him on Radio Banja Luka, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can I suggest that he said words to this effect and ask whether you heard this: All the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, he said he didn't hear him on the radio and now she is asking him if he heard something she is going to read. He said he didn't hear it. So, already said he answered the question. So I don't think there's any basis for her now reading it to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: His exact words were I don't remember listening to him, and I'm now seeing if I can refresh his recollection by putting to him the words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also in line and along the pattern of the questions and answers that we have had over the last few days when the witness obviously needed his memory to be refreshed sometimes upon his request. Yes, Ms. Korner, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That he said this: "All the decisions have been adopted. Every single one that has been passed is now in effect, and I now have the opportunity to say again on the radio to all those who have received them that they were supposed to implement them, and those who have failed to implement them will probably bear consequences ranging from their removal to responsibility." Do you remember hearing Mr. Brdjanin on Radio Banja Luka saying anything like that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to ask you just briefly, and we're nearly finished, about a woman known generally as Perka. You were asked about her in the first interview at page 60 to 61. In the B/C/S, it will be -- can we just check that Mr. Radic is given the first interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, can I ask if the quote that Ms. Korner just read from Banja Luka Radio comes from a document that's an exhibit in this case, and if so, what is its exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It does come from a document that is an exhibit in this case. It is -- just a moment, I'll just check. Sorry, Your Honour, I should have made a note. It's P2326, and it's the entry for the 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, both of you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. It was page 60 of the first interview, and it's 61 in the B/C/S. And it should be highlighted, I think. You were asked whether you you'd heard of a travel agency called Perka. And your answer was this: "That was not a travel agency. That was a scumbag from Zenica, and he did what he did here." Forgetting the next bit. But I think we're in cross-purposes. Who were you referring to as a scumbag? And I hope that's a proper translation of what you said.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to Perka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A woman?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And she came from Zenica to Banja Luka, did she?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that she came from Zenica. Because at the time there were quite a few refugees from Zenica, but I can't claim for certain that she was from Zenica. But it is certain that she wasn't from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you went on to say words to the effect that Perka had to report to the authorities anyone who had authority or was in a position to gain authority had to be supported by the higher ones: Then you were asked: "Who did Perka have to report to?" "To those who had to pay every time they got money from Muslims and Croats." You were asked: "Who was that?" And you said: "No one here." And then your answer: "I can't tell you exactly who she gave money to in Pale, but whoever it must have been, whoever allowed her to do this, but she had police protection, she had all kinds of protection but the police knew it all." And then, if I can summarise the rest because it's quite a long entry, you went on to say: No one could say anything to her. We tried to remove her but we couldn't. "Who tried to remove her?" "We did. We tried to remove her because this was a woman who came from Zenica to do whatever she did here." You were asked who you meant by "we." And you said: "We in the municipality; we knew. We tried to remove her because this was a madam who did not even pay taxes or anything else. And we weren't allowed to do anything. So she continued with her activities." "She was extorting money, correct, from non-Serbs?" "Extorting or not, it was illegal." "Okay. Did you report that to the CSB in Banja Luka?" "They all knew it." "Who knew it all?" "Those who protected her." And you went on to say you asked for her removal. Now, is that right, Mr. Radic? First of all, did you say that to us?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that right? You as the municipality president wanted to remove this woman because she was extorting money but she was being protected by somebody?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, we had a man who had been appointed by the municipality, and anyone who wanted to leave Banja Luka would report to this person. But this person told me that such an agency existed. That's what they called themselves, an agency. And this Mrs. Perka was in the agency. She would take money from those people. Are you listening or...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, they called themselves an agency, and Mrs. Perka was in that agency, and they would take money from people who wanted to leave Banja Luka. As to who she gave money to, I don't know. But we warned the CSB because only they could have prohibited -- prevented them from working because at the time we didn't have the SJB. We informed them that they should prevent her from operating. But this wasn't done. I can only assume that someone protected her and that it was in their interest to protect her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea who that was? Do you have any idea who that was? And I apologise, Mr. Radic. I was asking for a name. That's why I turned to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who was it? Someone who had an interest in that matter and someone who had enough power to protect that woman and allow her to do what she shouldn't have done. There were many such cases in the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know about her colleague, a man named, I think, Milos Bojinovic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milos Bojinovic. There was someone called Bandic who worked with her. But Bojinovic, I couldn't tell you anything about Milos Bojinovic. But there was someone called Bandic who worked her, and he protected Mrs. Perka. Unfortunately he was from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you understand there was somebody called Perka and somebody else called Bandic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they worked in a company, in an agency. They formed an agency. They received people that take money and do what they did naturally. This was a difficulty because that could have been attributed to the municipality which had a person who dealt with such matters, a person to whom Bosniaks and Croats would go if they wanted to leave Banja Luka. And he did warn about her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these people running this Perka agency were taking advantage of people who were desperate to leave the municipality. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. I want then finally to look, please, Mr. Radic, at what you've told us about Mr. Brdjanin personally. I want you first of all, please, to have a look at page 23 for us in the English of the first interview. It's page 24 for you. And there you were asked this in the English line 11. I think it's line 7 in the B/C/S. "Mr. Brdjanin held extreme views about Muslims and Croats, didn't he?" And your reply was: "Mr. Brdjanin had a very big mouth, and he talked a lot. How much he influenced the entire climate with his speeches, that's another matter." You were asked: "Tell me about his speeches." And you said: "As deputy and as a president of the crisis staff, he had access to the media, to the TV, to the newspapers, to the radio." Question: "He spoke through them regularly, didn't he?" Your answer: "He would appear when he thought it was good for him to say something, and what he said you probably have on record." It was put to you that, in fact, he stated only 2 per cent of Muslims and Croats would be allowed to remain in the area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Is that not correct? And your reply was: "If that's what it says, then yes. Because he said so many things you'd really need documentation to recall everything he said. Just one thing, if you'll allow me, at that time in the territories of Bosnia, Herzegovina, and Croatia, there was a propaganda war going on, and one inflammatory statement would end up in another." And then it continued. And then put to you, "To go beyond propaganda, Mr. Brdjanin had the authority as president of the ARK to cause events to occur in the local municipalities. Correct?" Your answer: "I don't know what you're referring to. I doubt that he could have caused anything, but let's see what you're talking about." Question: "Well, I'm asking you. Did you agree with his extreme views against non-Serbs?" And your reply: "I did have problems with him. But I resolved those directly. I would go to the TV, I'd go to the radio and confront him." Over the next page: "What discussions did you have with Mr. Brdjanin about his extreme views?" "Ugly ones." "Okay, tell me about those," was the question. "I cannot begrudge him saying things against mixed marriages. In any case - you then told us we had everything written down - everything was taped and recorded, and as I said, I had huge problems trying to calm it down in Banja Luka." Question: "And you would identify him as an extreme nationalist, would you not?" Answer: "He's not much more, he's not much of a nationalist." Question: "Was he extreme in his views against non-Serbs?" "In what his views were, I couldn't tell. But what he said, yes, he was a nationalist. But again, it was like a competition, who would spit the furthest." And then you went on to tell us that you had Sarajevo television, HTV, and this was just a reaction. Do you remember saying that to us?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you stand by what you said to us?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he had a big mouth? Yes. I stand by that. And that he would be opposed to what came from Sarajevo and from the HTV, Croatian television. But with the permission of the Trial Chamber, it's difficult for me to connect what he said about mixed marriages and the fact that he would save mixed marriages at the same time in Banja Luka. In the evening, he would talk against mixed marriages, and then the following morning he would try to save the marriage of a mixed pair. So it's difficult to make a connection between these two things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I think what you told us earlier, was that: That in private, he would sometimes help out Muslims and Croats. This was in evidence, Mr. Radic, not in the interview. But he couldn't say -- he couldn't talk about that openly because of his position. I can read you the exact words that you said if you like.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's something that I have also stated here. When you asked me about it, I said that he probably thought that it would be dangerous and that they would probably have removed him from all his positions if he had made such public statements, if he had stated this in public and if he had done these things in public.
