utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, because it was quite impossible in the climate of those days for any public figure to admit that there was anything good to be said about Muslims or Croats. Isn't that the situation?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't have been healthy to behave in such a way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you look, please, now at, for you, page 49 of the first interview, and for us page 48. It's lines 33 to 34. I'm sorry, it's the top of that page. Yes, 48 or 49. It's -- sorry, I ought to get back to. You were being asked at the bottom of our page 47 how many times you attended the meetings of the crisis staff, and you said rarely. And then you said somebody put to you a dozen -- I'm sorry. Yes, it was suggested: "Do you mean once or twice or a dozen?" And you said: "A dozen, please." And you said, I'm sorry, the question was: "What?" And you said: "A dozen please, maybe two or three times. To tell you the truth, I thought this was an illegitimate body, and I had many more urgent things to do. And to tell you the truth, Mr. Brdjanin imposed himself on the whole situation. His style was something I could just not accept." Did you say that to us?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm looking for it. You said 47 and 48, but I'm now trying to find the place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's page 48.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 48, yes, I've got it in front of me now. As far as these meetings are concerned, you said they were held in the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not, it's -- if you go on one more page, I think it must be page 49. I'm sorry, it should have been marked.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's highlighted in yellow. I considered, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I want simply to know also this: When you say his style was something you couldn't accept, what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes these were meetings which had no agendas. And in the course of the meeting, certain things would be changed and subjects that weren't at all on the agenda were discussed. I wasn't used to working in such a way. And I didn't attend these meetings. When I attend a meeting, I like to know what the agenda it. I like to know what the subjects are, and I like to go to deal with the subjects item by item. That was the usual way we would work, and that is why I did not attend these meetings. And I didn't notice that they were dealing or trying to resolve serious matters at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then that's all I want to ask you in the first interview. Could you have the second interview now, please, on this topic. And go to page 8. In the B/C/S, it's -- just a moment. Yes, it's 8 in both, I think. It's a very long answer you gave. You were asked about his speeches. And in fact, what had happened was you had been read his speech on the 12th of May assembly 1992 where he had said that various people should be removed. And you said: "Well, you can see for yourself from his speech how much the leading officials, how much attention they paid to his speeches because Karadzic, after speeches of" -- Karadzic used to say: "Well, Brdjanin has scored" - it says "a goal" -- "own goal" . Very much on the lines of that telephone conversation we listened to a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't say that. He didn't say "own goals". Yes, that he scored against himself, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. All right. And then you went on to explain various things in particular about Mr. Ruzic of the HDZ. And you said down, further Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. down: "I told you last time, and I'll tell you this time, Brdjanin didn't get his authority from the crisis staff but from the fact that he was a deputy. And if you're asking me if I was present at this gathering - that's the 12th of May assembly - I wasn't because it was only the deputies that were invited to such gatherings. He was also minister later on, even vice-president of the government, but for construction and communal public utilities. And these are the functions where he got his authority from. And this is where he, the position he acted from when he used to come here. And as far as this is concerned - actually referring back to the speech - there are far worse that he used to say. But I have to tell you that the majority of the Serbian people in Banja Luka did not support this and used to say that Brdjanin's tongue was longer than himself." And then you made a comment about his height. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the worst things that he used to say, if you can remember them?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what he had to say about mixed marriages, I think that's what they reproached him with the most, when he would say this wasn't desirable, when he said that mixed marriages weren't desirable. This affected the way we understood things, it violated the sanctity of marriage, especially if there were children, et cetera. But if I think back to everything, well, he would usually respond to provocations that came from Sarajevo television at the time, HTV, Croatian television, was very trenchant. We were able to follow their programme because we were within -- would receive it. But the subject, if you're asking me about the subject, with your permission, Your Honours, he'd probably respond now to Mr. Alispahic if the situation were at present and would say that we were genetic result of the Turks. It was an ugly language, and Mr. Brdjanin did these things. If you have other records, transcripts, et cetera, well, I can't remember everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reality of it was, wasn't it, Mr. Radic, and you realised that, was that these types of speeches made by a man in Mr. Brdjanin's position were absolutely terrifying for the non-Serbs in Banja Luka and everywhere else in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, madam. But on the other hand, they were also terrifying for all the Serbs in Sarajevo, all the Serbs in Croatia. It was just a reaction of Brdjanin as a Serb to what was being said in Zagreb and Sarajevo. Yes, it was terrifying, indeed it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you look on, please, in that second interview to page 54, you talked there about the subject you already mentioned to us. The dangers. I'm sorry. It's page 54 in English. In B/C/S, it's page 49 at the bottom, and over to page 50. You were asked: "Was it a very risky business?" I'll wait until it comes up on the screen. You were asked: "Was it a very risky business, dangerous for a Serb to help a Muslim or Croat during the period of time we're talking about?" You said: "Yes, it was. For example, for instance, I had a friend in Doboj, and I had to secure through the president of the ICRC in Doboj to forward some food to him because it was enough for them to label you as someone who was helping the Muslims and you were - I think it must be at their mercy, or out of their mercy. The same things happens to the people who were helping the Serbs in Sarajevo and Zagreb." "I know, that's true. But again, in this area, who did you perceive? Where was the danger coming from as a Serb to help a Muslim or Croat family in this city here? Where was the danger coming from, the danger that you felt?" "From my own national core" . "So from your own people?" "My own people. Everybody is my own people. But the Serbs, if they, if he finds out that I'm helping the Muslims, you know, if he knows and he's going to say it, I know how much hassle I had because I helped Mr. Ruzic. And for example, Colonel Hasotic who will not come to testify, I had to be very careful of what I was doing when I was helping him because everybody had forgotten what Mladic had said about him, that he was a good soldier and that he was willing to fight but it was to no avail." Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you now move to page 51 in your version and 56 for us. You were dealing with -- you talked about Bishop Komarica and what happened in 1993 and 1995, Operation Flash. You were then asked this: "When people disobeyed instructions from Pale within this region, were they generally removed?" "Well, at least they would go through what I went through in S93."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: September.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: September. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "They would be called in, they would go through ironing but some of them would be replaced straight on. And you were asked: Ironing. You mean things would be straightened out with the person?" "I don't know." And you replied: "I was -- you know very well what `ironing' means But it's not a tepid iron, either. It's a very hot one." And then the -- you were asked about Colonel Hasotic. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But Hasotic was not ironed or grilled by anybody. He's still in Banja Luka, and we are good friends, although I must tell you that even today I have to be very careful when I choose venues where I'm going to meet him. He is a man from Sandzak who said I am not going back to Sandzak. I have come to Banja Luka and this is where I am staying. And Indeed he has stayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even today, there are problems, aren't there, of maintaining friendships. Serbs and other nationalities?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only in Banja Luka, but also in Sarajevo and elsewhere. It is not healthy, to put it this way, for friends of different ethnic backgrounds to get together. This is still an undesirable situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, finally, and this is the last topic. I want to go back to where I started, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Korner. Mr. Ackerman, how are you for redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it looks like 30, 30 to 40 minutes, something in that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm only going to be 5 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can utilise whatever time is left, leaving, of course, Mr. Ackerman what he said he requires. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to have back the first interview for a moment, please. At page 71 for you, line 31, and then it goes over to page 72. Page 70 for us.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Am I supposed to look at the top of the page or the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It should be highlighted, page 71 starting at line 31, I hope. First interview. It's the part that begins after -- you were being asked -- again, effectively what you talked about in the second interview, September 1993. You were asked: "What other issues did you disagree with about things that were happening in Banja Luka or the ARK?" And your reply: "They always said that I was separatist, that I wanted to secede the western part from Republika Srpska." Question: "You wanted Banja Luka to be the capital of a separate state. That's right?" "That was not the basic goal, but that came later. I just could not agree as mayor. As the mayor, I could not agree with people coming down from the hills and doing what they did in Banja Luka." And I think what's been left out, and can we just check, is: "Take for example, Mrs. Plavsic." Is that in the B/C/S? It has been left out in the English, I think.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I read what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, just a moment. I'm not sure we're looking at the right... Yes, Plavsic. If you look at page 72 at the top, line 4, I think it doesn't come out in the English, but you said look what happened to Mrs. Plavsic or words -- "take, for example, Mrs. Plavsic."

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we just read on. You were asked: "Was there a meeting at some stage in Banja Luka between you, Karadzic, and Krajisnik when Karadzic was saying to you that Banja Luka hadn't been properly ethnically cleansed?" In other words, that they were blaming you that there were still Muslims and Croats in Banja Luka. Your answer: "That was not just once. That happened a lot. But I can't recall exactly when they said all that. But that objection was made against me." Question: "And you say that was more than once?" Answer: "Whenever we would meet, somebody would object to the fact that there were too many of them. It was too many for them and for the Muslims and Croats, not enough so." And then you were asked: "So you were aware that the creation of the Republika Srpska did involve the deportation of Muslims and Croats?" And you said: "Not necessarily. If the same hadn't happened on the other side." And then you went on to deal with that. And on the same page, you dealt with the fact that the deportation was not a voluntary one. Now, do you remember saying that to us, Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would be very grateful to you if we could read the entire text, between 17 and 23, the paragraph that you have just omitted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. I'm perfectly happy to do that. "Not necessarily. If the same hadn't happened on the other side, I keep trying" -- Your Honour, in the original it says "I." It says are you, but it does, we checked that. "I keep trying to tell people that when I received 45.000 Serbs from Slavonia and Banja Luka in December of 1991, that that had to have been reflected in the demographic structure of Banja Luka. When 250.000 Serbs from the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Knin came here -- come here and they still haven't left, how can you expect an unchanged and unaltered demographic structure." Do you want me to read on, Mr. Radic, or is that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is sufficient to get the whole picture and put things in perspective. So it was nobody's will to move people from this area, to cleanse people. If you first receive 45.000, and then 250.000, then even those who live there, the non-Serb population, cannot feel at ease. And if you will allow me to say another thing, if there hadn't been Mr. Samaruga and if he hadn't seen what was going on when the exodus of Serbs started from Croatia, God knows what would have happened in Banja Luka in 1995 when these people were all armed and if they had entered the city centre they would have torn it apart. And what would have happened to the non-Serb population is very hard for me to begin to imagine. However, they were diverted, and redirected to go around Banja Luka so they were prevented from the town itself. This is what I had in mind when I said this, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But effectively, what you were telling us there was that Karadzic and Krajisnik were saying "you are not ethnically cleansing Banja Luka properly" and you were saying "it is quite impossible to do that because of the numbers of refugees." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm wondering if you would be willing to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then I can complete after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Radic. You are going to be asked a few more questions by Mr. Ackerman arising out of the cross-examination. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, the first document we're going to look at is -- was shown to you by the Prosecutor. It's -- I don't think the usher is going to need to find it. I think we might be able to do this all with Sanction if I can run it and if I get some help from the booth. Yes, it's coming up. You'll recall Document P2698 was that document from the journalist, Milos Vasic I think was his name, that you were asked about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this is in English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know it's in English. And there's nothing we can do about that. You're not going to be able to read it. The reason I'm bringing it up is so everybody else can see it. And I'm going to have to read the parts to you that I want to refer to. And it will be translated for you as I read it. So the part I'm interested in is this: "Gangs of renegades, paramilitary formations, are roaming through Eastern Bosnia with total disregard for anything or anyone, including the Serbian government agents describing themselves as commanders of the local Territorial Defence. The leaders of the group, at least ten are known to exist, openly say they have no intention of ever returning to Serbia where they could face trial for war crimes. Their objective is to settle down one day and become high-ranking officials in a future Karadzic government. Murder, hostage-taking, looting, the expulsion of people from their homes have become probably so normal that even the combat morale of Karadzic's troops has suffered. The president of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina no longer controls his troops, and neither does General Ratko Mladic who said so two weeks ago." This paragraph that I read to you talks about -- describes a situation that sounds of almost complete chaos and anarchy going on at the time. Was that the case? Was it pretty much chaos and anarchy going on at the time?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, what is described here is Eastern Bosnia, whereas we were in Western Bosnia. However, I sincerely doubt that these and such people could do whatever they wanted to do, given the fact that Ratko Mladic was there. And especially if those were formations such as described in here. Ratko Mladic could not support and could not tolerate an army with ethnic characteristics. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me see if I understand what you just told us. Are you telling us that there were these out-of-control groups that Mladic simply could not tolerate? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I said that I don't know what was going on in Eastern Bosnia, in Podrinje and in Romanija and in the hills out there. We were in the western part in Bosanska Krajina, so I don't know what was going on there. However, I express my doubt as to the fact that Mr. Ratko Mladic who later on became a general would allow them to go wild there. Especially, he did not tolerate an army with ethnic characteristics. He would, for example, snatch those Chetnik insignia from their hats and stomp on those with their feet. You know what Chetnik insignia I'm talking about, those that they used to wear on their caps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there, and this will be my final question about this and we'll go to this next section that I want to talk to you about. Were there groups operating, paramilitary groups operating in the Krajina area that were out of control, not under the control of General Talic or the police, just sort of renegade bands, basically, of criminals? Was that happening? That's my question. Was that happening in 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an attempt. However, they were very soon either brought in by the military or they would run away. Because General Talic told them loud and clear that they should either return to the barracks, put on uniforms, take weapons, and go to the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you told us that's his position with regard to the SOS when he came back from the corridor after they had opened the corridor, that what he told the SOS people was they had to either join the corps or go away. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Those who didn't want to do that fled to Belgrade, did there whatever they did. They tried to return. And one of them in a conflict with the police got killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second part I want from this same article that I want to ask you about reads as follows: "The Bosnian Krajina on the other hand was always politically autonomous, often widely at variance with the policies of Karadzic with who it should by definition be in total agreement. This is understandable. They're historically and in many other ways two different regions. Apart from this, Karadzic happens to be physically distant." Is that an accurate statement in this article?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, this was the case. Bosnian Krajina was far away from the centre, from Sarajevo and Pale, and it strived towards some sort of an autonomy. And it tried to affirm this autonomy by establishing an assembly, by introducing their on constitution. I am saying an attempt was made, but this attempt was thwarted on the day when the assembly was supposed to sit for the first time. Obviously, a lot of people used that to portray it as a conflict between the Serbs in the west and the Serbs in the east.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said -- you told us that -- going back now to that first part we referred to, that early on, there were these attempts by groups that were out of control. I think you called them "attempts." Yesterday, you'll recall that you were shown a document by Ms. Korner. It's Exhibit P35. We don't need to look at it again today because you'll know exactly what I'm talking about. This was from the Serb --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you remind me of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It came from the Serb club of deputies. And Ms. Korner and the Judge were both asking you about it. There was a statement in there: "Establish immediately strict control of the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was actually an assembly, not the club of deputies. An assembly meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The deputies is 29. This is 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, this is 35. I was wrong about that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remember that statement in that document, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard a lot of things now. Are you talking about the club, about the Assembly of Krajina, or the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska? What are we talking about here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it was the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. The document was P35. You were asked about it at length yesterday. There was one phrase in there that said: "Establish immediately strict control of the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." I'm just asking you if you remember being asked about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you remember I told you it means take control -- effectively take control of the territory. And you told me no, there is a difference between take control and establish control. Then you proceeded -- do you remember now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, to establish control, and that was my precise answer. Control over the territory, because the question was whether this was control over people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now bearing in mind what we have been talking about the last few minutes, about these groups that were trying to -- making attempts, as you say, to -- out of the control of the army, out of the control of the police, the language "establish immediately strict control of the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina," Ms. Korner suggested that meant to take strict control over the non-Serb areas, that strict control should be established over those areas. Let me ask you if that's the only conclusion one could draw from this directive, or can it have meant taking control of those places that were in chaos and anarchy at the time?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained to Madam Prosecutor that we had to establish the control over the territory. Why? Because the military had already concentrated on the banks of the Sava River and on the banks of the Una on the Croatian side. Secondly, there were individuals who tried to establish their own army. This is not what I said to Ms. Korner. One such unit would line up every morning in the parking lot by the municipal assembly building. I warned the military, and they were then asked to join the regular troops. Those who wanted to join the regular troops were given uniforms; those who didn't, they had to surrender their weapons. They had to return whatever uniforms they had and leave the area. One more thing I would like to say: That particular unit got involved in war operations. And when these young men were wounded, their parents came knocking on my door to ask me who would be in charge of their treatment and who would compensate them. I referred them to the person, to the commander who took them into the battle without any authorisation. Then, that person realised that it was not the right thing to do, to take these men without any authority into a battle where they could be injured or where they could be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We're going to be here a long time if you spend that much time answering each of my questions. We'll be here until sometime Monday, so please try to do your best, and I'll try to do my best, although I'm having a little trouble technologically right now. I want you to look at another document. It's -- I'll get it here in just a second. Don't worry, it's coming. Now, the other day when I was showing you a document from the Prijedor Municipality that had to do with Prijedor not being willing to follow the orders of the ARK Crisis Staff, I showed you the wrong document. I'm now showing you P1261. And if you have trouble reading it, I can make it bigger for you.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please enlarge it. I can't see very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whoops, that's not it. All right.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here in this conclusion, and that supports the claim that they wanted to be autonomous with respect to the regional crisis staff, and that that municipal crisis staff would not accept the decisions taken before the 22nd of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, it says, doesn't it, that they won't honour any until after June 22nd, 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the major question here is do you think that Prijedor felt like they had to implement all the decisions of the ARK Crisis Staff or that they had -- that they had the power to choose which ones they thought they wanted to implement?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This clearly shows what the case was. They said they wouldn't implement decisions taken before the 22nd of June. So it is obvious that they adopted decisions without referring to the ARK Crisis Staff. That's what I said when I spoke about municipalities said -- did what they wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Ms. Korner was talking to you today about implementation, she kept using the word "orders" from the ARK Crisis Staff. And did they follow orders? Did they implement orders? Do you recall ever seeing a document from the ARK Crisis Staff that was called an "order"?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in your testimony yesterday, I think it was yesterday, you were talking about -- and I think I asked you about it even, that -- you talked about the people in Prijedor being too powerful for Brdjanin, and you were asked about that. And you said: "Not only were they too powerful for Brdjanin, they were too powerful for even some other institutions of government. They had a sort of autonomy of their own. I would like to remind you that even before the war, they asked to be a subregion, not to be part of the region of Bosanska Krajina." Now, in connection with that response of yours, I want you to look at another document. And this is P247, I believe. Now, this is a document from what's called the Sanska Unska area. And it was a meeting of representatives from Srpska Krupa, Bosanski Petrovic, Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Dubica, Prijedor, and Sanski Most. The part I'm interested in having you look at is -- let me get it on the screen for you.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know. I'm a little slow, but I'll get there. Let's see. I think we probably got there. If you look at 3(a), and if you need me to make this bigger for you, I can make it bigger for you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Make it bigger straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please enlarge it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Probably the best thing to do now is for you just to read it out loud, and then it will get translated. But read very slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sure we all remember this document. We don't need to have it read out loud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him read it, because I can't see the English version like this. So at least I will have a translation of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I suggest that instead of Mr. Ackerman playing with his technological marvels, we go straight back to ordinary exhibits. It's quicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It might be. But sometimes it takes a long time to find the document and give it to the witness. But if, if the -- the Registrar wants to find PT47 and give it me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, we're wasting time. Mr. Radic, read those few lines, please, in your own language, and someone will have them translated to us. Not someone, I mean the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Your Honours, these technological advances shouldn't be to my detriment. I wouldn't want to be here on Monday. Let me read it. "The common conclusions at the meeting in Banja Luka on the 15th of June 1992." Since you have warned me of this Mr. Ackerman. "I considered that the crisis staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina" -- and now you have made it smaller again. "So the common conclusions of the session in Banja Luka on the 15th of June 1992. (A), we believe that the crisis staff of the ARK has to work in wartime conditions in a more serious way and with greater political and professional sense for the problems in all municipalities that constitute the Autonomous Region of Krajina. "(B), in this sense we suggest that the president of the Crisis Staff of the ARK be Vojo Kupresanin by virtue of his position as president of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. "(C), all the sessions of the crisis staff of the ARK should in future be held with a tape recorder and some court reporters." And there is nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The first question I have about that is that's, I think, what you were talking about as the subregion that the Prijedor Municipality was part of and interested in being part of. And the question I have for you about that, that indicates, does it not, that there was dissension among that group, at least, against the operation of the crisis staff of the autonomous region and especially against Brdjanin as its head?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't objected as yet. Every single one of these questions is leading. Every single one of these comments -- I'm making a speech again. It's not re-examination

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed, Ms. Korner. We will finish earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ackerman, I think that this was demonstrated more by the list of municipalities that you showed in which a request was made for them to be a subregion of Prijedor at its head. But on the basis of this, I couldn't conclude that that is what it means. Why did they ask for Kupresanin instead of Brdjanin? On the basis of this short passage, I couldn't say. But it is obvious that there is something they weren't satisfied with as far as Brdjanin is concerned, and this is why they requested Kupresanin. What you showed me was far more indicative, when they said that they were asking for a subregion with municipalities. Prijedor, Dubica, and Novi Krupa, et cetera. That's the subregion before the war that existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, have you been given this document now in its original form? If you try to find this same page that's on the screen and look at the paragraph right at the very bottom. That's the next paragraph I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That happens to do with the representatives of Krupa, et cetera, were present. And under (e) it says: "We believe that the functioning of the crisis staff hasn't been satisfactory to date and that it is being reduced to the Banja Luka local interest. The crisis staff in our opinion should be formed by the Municipal Assembly and the representatives of the SDS in all the municipalities that form the ARK." Is that what you were referring to, Mr. Ackerman? That is (e).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm looking at actually -- paragraph (e) is what you just looked at. But look at paragraph (f) now, please. I think it's the next.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The work of the Serbian Democratic Party must make itself felt, especially during these hard times of war. So far, we have been dissatisfied with the work of the regional board of the Serbian Democratic Party in Banja Luka." That is (f).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then there's one paragraph after that that starts with the "accordingly, personnel changes should be made in the crisis staff." Do you see that? I don't think you need to read it out. Just...

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph is that? (g), (h)?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the next one. It's the paragraph between what you just read from (f) and paragraph (g).

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It speaks about urgently breaking with individuals who have decided to obstruct the work of the Serbian Democratic Party in the Autonomous Region of Krajina and to question the lofty goals which have galvanised the Serbian people. Now, who do you think that would be referring to, requesting personnel changes in the crisis staff and getting rid of people who are obstructing the work of the Serbian Democratic Party in ARK? Who would that be referring to in the context of everything else we've seen in this document?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, it's difficult for me to say who they're referring to. It is obvious that they are not satisfied with the work of the members of the crisis staff of ARK at the time. They don't say who should be replaced, but it is obvious that they requested that some people be replaced if they thought that they were not sufficiently engaged, not sufficiently involved in implementing the SDS's positions. But who they're referring to, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we saw earlier in the document that they were asking that Mr. Kupresanin take over as head of the crisis staff. Who would he be replacing if he did that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He'd replace Brdjanin who was the president of the crisis staff. So they wanted to bring in Kupresanin. Brdjanin was the president of the crisis staff at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your cross-examination by Ms. Korner, you were asked about a document. It's Exhibit P97. You'll remember it, I'm sure. It's the document that had -- that she showed you that had the variants A and B -- variant A depending on -- for a Serb majority municipality; variant B for a minority municipality. Do you remember that document?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to see that document. I've really seen a lot of documents, so I can no longer remember which one is concerned since five days have passed. If you have such a document, I would like to see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will get it to you in a moment.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very vaguely, but I would like to see it. Mr. Ackerman, could you please tell me the page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's no page I'm interested in. I just want you to be familiar that -- I'm just asking you if you remember being shown that document.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can't read it, how can I know whether I've seen it? There's variant A, first level, et cetera. I have the impression that I've seen this document, but I'm not quite sure what your question concerns, so I'd be glad to answer it, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me see if you can remember, and if not, fine, we'll go on to something else. You said in your examination yesterday, Ms. Korner asked you about that document. You said: "It was delivered to all municipalities." And my question is how would you know it was delivered to all municipalities? How could you possibly know that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, which document? Please tell me finally. I'd like to see the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The one you are looking at. That's the document.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the one I'm looking at, it consists of four pages. The entire document?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The entire document.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian Democratic Party, Bosnia-Herzegovina, the main board, yes, of course, it was forwarded to everyone. It was forwarded to everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question I have is how you would know that it was forwarded to everyone? On what are you basing that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because the Serbian Democratic Party in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the main board, strictly confidential, copy number, et cetera, et cetera, was probably forwarded to everyone. Instructions for the functioning of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It must have been forwarded to everyone. You see it says copy number 100 here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're just assuming that it was forwarded to everyone? You don't know?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's highly probable that everyone received this because this is a document which refers to the organisation and activity of the organs of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't know what else I can tell you. That's the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's clear. His answer is clear enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, I'd like you to look now at Document P272, please. And I'll let the usher get it for you. This will be I think the third time that you have been shown this document. Ms. Korner showed it to you today as an example - is this the right one, yes - as an example of how decisions of the ARK Crisis Staff were implemented in various places. What I want to do is draw your attention -- this is a document that was circulated actually by Stojan Zupljanin. I want to draw your attention to the second page of that document under the number 3 where it reads as follows: "However, employees may not be dismissed or removed from posts without the knowledge of the Security Services Centres, though the contrary has been done in some stations. Adequate solutions to their appointments and duty assignments which do not contradict item 1 of the decision must be sought out." My question is, does this document show that the police are implementing the decision of the ARK Crisis Staff or that they are not implementing a decision of the ARK Crisis Staff unless they wish to? And what does this say here? What is Zupljanin telling the chiefs in the various local police stations?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, on the first page, it says that the CSB Banja Luka is sending this, the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka. I'd like to see the decision if there is one, which is the original decision from the AR Krajina Crisis Staff. It refers to the crisis staff decision that's on the first page. But on the second page, it says that it should not be implemented without him being aware of it. So he's saying that there are other solutions and that this should not be done without his knowledge. That's what I said yesterday, too. And I stand by what I said yesterday. Mr. Zupljanin took the liberty not to follow what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I now want to -- I'm finished with that. I want to ask you about something from your second statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. And it's on page 51 in English. And I don't have the B/C/S version, so I am not going to be able to find it for you. But I think if you had the English version and looked at page 51, I could -- it's a very short thing that I want you to see. This has to do with your visit to Omarska and you're going to see Mr. Schweitzer about that, upon your return to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think page 46 or 47 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think we really need the B/C/S. I think we can get through this rather quickly if we just find page 51 of the English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're being asked about the visit to Omarska. And starting at line 6 on page 51, you say: "I went to the ICRC and asked Meaning or Schweitzer - I don't know who was the boss then - you know, get them out of there." And Mr. Cayley said: "We know. We know you did. We know you did." Did you get the impression when during that exchange that what Mr. Cayley was telling you was that the Prosecutor's office knew that you had gone to Mr. Schweitzer and reported to Mr. Schweitzer what you saw at Omarska, that they knew that from independent sources? Is that the impression you got?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I have to say that I didn't ask myself how he obtained that information and what the fact that he knew that I had spoken to Mr. Schweitzer meant. I don't know who told him about that. I don't know where he found out that I had spoken about this. I don't know whether he received a document from the Red Cross. But it's obvious that the man said that he knew. And I didn't ask myself how it is that he knew this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, okay, I'm finished with that. Earlier today you indicated that Mr. Brdjanin had spoken against -- spoken out against mixed marriages. I want you to think about that a bit. If you had known that eight members of Mr. Brdjanin's family, including his two brothers, are in mixed marriages and were at the time, do you think it would have been Mr. Brdjanin who would have said that or might it have been Dr. Vukic who made that statement and you'd just gotten confused?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, I'd be happiest if Brdjanin, Mr. Brdjanin said whether he spoke about against mixed marriages. But this is what you could hear in Banja Luka, and many inhabitants of Banja Luka can confirm this. But Mr. Vukic also spoke about these mixed marriages. But unfortunately, Mr. Brdjanin also spoke about this. And that's why I've said that it was very strange for him to speak against mixed marriages on television, but he would save Mr. Miskin and Mrs. Miskin's mixed marriage. But yes, Mr. Vukic also spoke about this since you have mentioned him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next question I want to ask you is about the testimony about Mr. Karadzic criticising you for not properly ethnically cleansing Banja Luka basically. And you said that that happened on more than one occasion. What was the latest occasion in time that you can remember, the month and the year if you can, that you received that kind of criticism?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly when this criticism was addressed at me. But it never happened that I would meet either him or one of his associates and when I wouldn't be said that everything that Banja Luka had done was okay except for this problem. There are transcripts which show what the conversations between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Brdjanin were like in that respect. And I believe that your question is simply out of place, and there's no need to ask me when this was said to me. You must have transcripts. I was told many times how come I was not cleansing the banks, how I was not cleansing other institutions, and they even suggested I should be removed because of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, my question is did this happen after 1992? Did this happen 1993? Were you criticised in 1993 for Banja Luka not being properly cleansed?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Banja Luka was amongst the last towns which was ethnically cleansed. The same went for mosques. And it was an ongoing criticism at my address as the president of the municipal assembly. I was always criticised for doing things very slowly, for not cleansing the banks of people whose names were mentioned. Now, when you're asking me whether this was in 1991, 1993, 1992, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You just told us that Banja Luka was one of the last towns that was ethnically cleansed. When was it that most of the non-Serb population that actually decided to leave, when was it that the vast bulk of them left? What year?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: It started already at the moment when the Serbs from Western Slavonia on the 15th of December came in huge numbers to Banja Luka. Then they started arriving from Travnik. Others were people who were expelled from Travnik, from Bugojno, from Zenica, from Sarajevo, and so on and so forth. The bulk of the people left in May 1995 during the Operation Flash and Storm. That was in August and September when 250.000 Serbs from Banja Lika, Kordon and so on and so forth, started moving towards Banja Luka and via Banja Luka. Even Mr. Samaruga at that point felt the danger and had an agreement signed with Mr. Koljevic about voluntary displacement of the non-Serbian people from this area. He was afraid because these people came very heavily armed. They took all their weapons with them, and they started moving towards Banja Luka and Serbia. Even to this very day, there are very many of them in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You already told us about that today. And I really want you to be able to go home. My real question was when did the bulk of the non-Serb people leave Banja Luka? When did the big bunch? Was it in 1991? Was it in 1995? Was it in 1993? You must know; you were the president of the municipality. When did large numbers of non-Serbs leave Banja Luka? Just give us a year. Don't give me a five-minute answer because you'll be here Monday?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been 1991, 1993, 1992 when they were losing their jobs, losing their livelihood. But most of them left at the end of the war when the Serbs had been expelled from Slavonia and the Republic of Serbian Krajina as its name was at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier today at the beginning of your testimony you were talking, in answer to Ms. Korner's questions, about the decision process in the ARK Crisis Staff. And you indicated that when it came down to it, Mr. Brdjanin always had the last word. My question is, if you only went to one or two meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff, how would you know that Mr. Brdjanin always had the last word? Or do you know? Were you just guessing or do you know?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, I said that I assume that it was Mr. Brdjanin because he presided over the crisis staff. I didn't say explicitly that it was always him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Chamber, I think, on a couple of occasions now since you have been here that Mr. Brdjanin's power, what power he had, came because of his role as a deputy, not from his role as president of the crisis staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that that power or that authority that he had as a deputy, would that have given him power to control the army or the police?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to -- when you were up in Prijedor after you'd gone to Omarska and you were then in Prijedor, do you recall Mr. Drljaca telling your group that after being criticised about what you'd seen at Omarska, do you recall him saying that "well, the people are there because we're trying to protect them from extremists who otherwise would be attacking them"? Do you recall him giving that kind of an excuse?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really do object to this. There are leading questions and there are leading questions. But that was just incredible, not to mention that there's no evidence of any of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, please refer him to chapter and verse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't have a document in that regard, Your Honour. I just am wondering if he remembers Mr. Drljaca saying anything like that. He can either say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, he can't. It's utterly objectionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am taking your objection, Ms. Korner. I am suggesting Mr. Ackerman another way out to try and find out from the witness what Mr. Drljaca may have said. Exactly. But I can't tell Mr. Ackerman how to phrase a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to withdraw the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just have one last thing, Mr. Radic: I appreciate your coming here, and I know you were here much longer than you were told that you would be here, than what you expected. And I think we all appreciate that you have gone through this process with us. I just want to ask you this: When you go back to Banja Luka, if you have any ability whatsoever to find the minutes from the ARK Crisis Staff, if you can find anyone who has them, if you can encourage anyone to locate them, we would desperately like to have them. So can you please try to do that. And with that, that's all I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was that a question, Mr. Ackerman, or -- the secretary who had already testified here, Mr. Blagojevic, should have those minutes. I really don't have them. I don't know where they were kept or whether there were any in the first place. I must tell you that I really doubt whether these minutes ever existed. There were not that many meetings in the first place, and I sincerely doubt that any written documents were kept. However, you should ask Mr. Blagojevic. Of course, if I ever found them, I would send them to you. There's no question about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One last thing. There was a book you wanted to present to the Trial Chamber. I assume you will get that to us. And thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will most certainly do that, to show you that the Serbs were not engaged in any propaganda war using the nine babies who died because of the lack of oxygen. You're going to get the book with all the names of the babies, of their parents. The doctor who authored the book sent it to all the presidents of all the states in the world to show them what was going on during the time when we were cut off. I'm going to do it. Most certainly I am. And if you will allow me, I would like to take the opportunity to say in the presence of the lady from Japan, that Mrs. Sadako Ogata also came to Banja Luka, and we showed that book to her as well when she visited us in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, we have a few more minutes before your ordeal is over. We have a few questions. Judge Janu will go first. Thank you. Because we really appreciate -- we join with what Mr. Ackerman said. Being here for five days testifying is an ordeal in itself. So we are thankful ourselves for your presence here and your testimony. Judge Janu, please. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I would like to take you back to the travel agency Perka. I know you told us that she didn't pay the taxes and other things. But we in this proceeding, we have heard, and it wasn't from the Prosecution side, that she was considered in Banja Luka something like Mother Theresa. Her services were appreciated by Muslims very much. Could you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't say that she didn't pay taxes. Because we didn't know how much she charged these people, and in any case, people like her did not pay taxes, and we did not want to collect taxes from them because her agency was not a legal establishment. Now, whether the Croats and Muslims were grateful to her, it's entirely their matter. It's up to them. And I also have to say, Your Honour, that there were also those who complained against her, saying that she had taken their money and that she didn't help them. So much about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you yourself, if I understood you well, provided some attempt that the municipality would organise or town would organise this transportation. If I am right, can you tell me the intention was to give these services, this transport freely to the Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely. This was under control, and the name of the person who did it is well known. He did it until the moment when such unauthorised agencies appeared and transported -- started transporting people. There was another agency in addition to this one. We reported them to the authorities in order to stop their illegal activities, but...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So there was a time when Perka and your service were in competition, both functioning?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can you have a competition with somebody who did not take money from Muslims or Croats? The only thing they did, they said to them how much the ticket would cost until the border. That was a regular agency who contacted Adalbert Rebic in Croatia and told him that there would be a certain number of people to be transported. And then Adalbert Rebic who was in charge of those matters on behalf of Croatia would receive them. As for this other agency, where was it that they sent these people I don't know. The person who was appointed by the executive council of the municipal assembly did that until the moment those illegal agencies appeared. When they realised that they could make a killing on these people and on those services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I just wanted to know if those people had a choice? You said your intention was to give this transportation freely, the municipality offered this, and Perka was charging enormous money. So I wanted to know if those services were both available for the people who wanted to leave. That was all what I was after. And my second, and please answer just very simply: Did you belong to the circle of the people who had free access to Radovan Karadzic? You could call him by the telephone directly? Because we know there are all those lines, preferential lines, with just special groups. So did you belong to those people? And how often did you call him to discuss the problems, if you remember roughly?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very rarely, Your Honour. The last time I spoke to him was when it was threatened that the bishop's house and cathedral would be destroyed. And then he blocked both the cathedral and the bishop's residences, and Bishop Komarica is aware of that and the paper represented it, and Mr. Montarisio is also aware of that. It was Mr. Karadzic who gave orders for the whole area to be blocked, to prevent this thing from happening. That's when I called Karadzic. I also called him when a Jewish couple was killed, when an aggravated murder was committed because somebody thought they had money. That's when I called him, and Mr. Ackerman's assistant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: I'm sorry to stop you, but I just wanted to know a rough number. We know from the discussion we heard here it was once with Mr. Vukic and Mr. Brdjanin. You said twice, this Jewish couple and another time. So three, four times? Can you estimate? Maybe you cannot.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not more than five times altogether. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge, the transcript at page 79 line 22, the transcript reveals that Mr. Radic said "they could make a killing," and I'm told he said: "They could make a living."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Makes a bit of a difference. Mr. Radic, before we conclude, I noticed that you were not asked, and of course you did not volunteer any remarks on the red combi? Do you remember that there was a red combi in Banja Luka in 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People from the CSB and the state security will be able to tell you much more about the red combi. This was something that was not discussed in Banja Luka at all. I wish I could have had this red van removed from the streets of Banja Luka. They didn't leave anybody alone, including the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So my question, was it a problem for you as the mayor of Banja Luka at the time?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A huge problem. But there was nobody that admitted to have anything to do with the red combi. Everybody denied any connection, although they had connections. But Mr. Brdjanin did not have any connections with that red combi. But gentlemen from the CSB and the state security should be able to tell you who was in that red van.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you try -- or what did you try as mayor with the power that you had at the time to get rid of this red combi? What did you try at the time?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got in contact with the most responsible people from the state security, from the CSB, asking them to take measures in order to eliminate this red van and the people who carried out all these actions. Every time I contacted them, they denied having anything to do with that red van.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I will not press the matter any further. On behalf of this Trial Chamber, Judge Janu, Judge Taya and myself, and on behalf of the Tribunal as a whole, I wish to thank you for having accepted to come here and give evidence as a Defence witness. I also wish to inform you, to confirm to you, that you will receive any -- all the assistance that you need, you require, to enable you to return home as quickly as possible. We've done our best, Ms. Korner and Mr. Ackerman, to make sure that you could leave before the weekend. So I thank you once more. You'll be escorted now by Madam usher. And our last words to you is we wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Monday we meet in the morning. The sitting is in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have one application in relation to this, and that is to make both interviews exhibits. We've gone through so much of them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you had already --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think I have. So if I could, Your Honour, could that be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. There's no point in even discussing it. They need to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, as I say, we have been through so much of it. Could the interview of 2001 become P2705, English A, B/C/S B -- whichever way it's done. I don't remember. And the 2002 interview P2706.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And who is coming first next week? Because I am in a little bit of a confusion. I had a statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Savic is coming first, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We had to switch them because of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay, because we got two statements via email, and one which we found on our desk yesterday. So I have three basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know anything about how one was found on your desk, but we did send a couple by email.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You should have Savic and I think it's Koljevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We found yesterday -- not on our desk, the statement of Witness Number 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's just a regular disclosure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And what is the plan, to have all these three witnesses next week, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just the two that we received by email.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We've only got four days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judging by the way we have been going so far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it depends. They are not as important witnesses or the same calibre as the witness that we had --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's for certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I wish you all a nice weekend. This was a difficult week. And I thank you for your cooperation. Thank you. See you Monday.
